title: Topic: Firm Performance and Growth
text:
These are the most commonly used outcome indicators in EU firm-level impact evaluations. Where possible, use administrative data (business registries, tax records) rather than self-reported figures to reduce measurement error.
###Turnover growth

Definition: Change in total annual sales revenue over the evaluation period
Metric: % change in turnover from baseline to endline; log of turnover
Data source: Administrative (tax records, business registry) or primary survey

###Value added

Definition: Value of output minus the value of intermediate inputs; a measure of the firm’s contribution to GDP
Metric: Total value added in € (turnover minus purchases of goods and services); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative (tax records) or primary survey

###Labour productivity

Definition: Output produced per unit of labour input — a core competitiveness indicator
Metric: Value added per employee (€); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative or primary survey (requires both value added and employment data)

###Total factor productivity (TFP)

Definition: Output not explained by inputs — captures how efficiently a firm uses all its resources
Metric: Estimated using production function methods (e.g. Olley-Pakes, Levinsohn-Petrin); requires data on output, capital, labour, and materials
Data source: Administrative (requires linked firm-level panel data)

###Employment growth

Definition: Change in the number of people employed by the firm
Metric: % change in full-time equivalent (FTE) employees from baseline to endline; log of employment
Data source: Administrative (social security records, business registry) or primary survey

###Wage growth

Definition: Change in average wages paid by the firm, reflecting improvements in job quality and productivity
Metric: % change in average gross wage per employee; total wage bill growth
Data source: Administrative (social security or tax records)

###Export performance

Definition: Whether and how much the firm sells in foreign markets
Metric: Export participation (yes/no); share of turnover from exports (%); log of export value
Data source: Administrative (customs data) or primary survey

###Firm survival

Definition: Whether the firm remains in operation over the evaluation period
Metric: Binary indicator (firm active / closed); survival rate across the sample
Data source: Administrative (business registry)

title: How
text:
Choosing the group size
To detect the impact of a programme, you need enough firms in both the treatment and comparison groups to reliably tell a real effect apart from the ordinary differences between firms. Statisticians call this statistical power: with too few firms, even a programme that works can appear not to. The smaller the effect you want to detect, the more firms you need. Rules of thumb and power calculations are covered in Advanced How.

Two ways to increase your sample


Loosen the eligibility bar
If fewer firms qualify than you’d like, lowering the eligibility threshold lets more firms into the pool you randomise from.


Widen the ranking bins
If you’re ranking firms by a score, don’t treat the ranking as exact. Group similarly-scored firms into bands, and treat everyone in a band as equally eligible, so more firms end up in the randomised pool rather than being decided by their exact rank.



A bigger pool also gives you room to test more than one version of the programme at once – more on that under Multiple treatment arms, below.

title: How
section: Five practical ways to randomise your programme
text:
Five practical ways to randomise your programme
Not every programme fits the same shape. Here are five common ways to randomise one.

  
    Lottery
    How: randomly select who gets the programme, by public or private lottery.
    Best when: eligibility is clear and the programme is oversubscribed.
  
  
    Multiple treatment arms
    How: randomly assign different versions of the programme, with or without a control group.
    Best when: you want to know which design works best, not just whether it works.
  
  
    Randomised phase-in
    How: everyone gets the programme eventually, in a random order. Those still waiting are the comparison group.
    Best when: budget or capacity cannot cover everyone at once.
  
  
    Randomised intensities
    How: vary how much of the programme a firm gets, for example 100%, 50%, or 0% of eligible employees.
    Best when: spillovers within or between firms are a concern.
  
  
    Encouragement design
    How: randomise who gets extra outreach to take up the programme, since it cannot be denied to anyone.
    Best when: take-up is voluntary and the programme itself cannot be withheld.
  


SMART Romania used a lottery
Of the five designs above, SMART Romania used a lottery: 1 038 eligible firms were randomly split into a treatment group of 519, invited to apply for a grant, and a comparison group of 519, not invited.

title: How
section: Running a lottery: transparency vs. behavioural responses
text:
Running a lottery: transparency vs. behavioural responses



Public lottery


A public draw, for example pulling names from a hat.
Advantage: transparent and fair.
Disadvantage: the comparison group may change its behaviour once it knows the result.




Private lottery


A lottery run behind the scenes.
Advantage: avoids the comparison group reacting to a public result.
Disadvantage: less visibly fair.




In practice, many World Bank-supported evaluations run the draw as a secure, documented, computerised procedure that can be re-checked afterwards.

Either kind of lottery can also be narrowed to just part of the pool: rather than randomising everyone who’s eligible, you can randomise only the firms near the eligibility cutoff, and decide the clear-cut cases directly.

title: How
text:
Rule-based scoring beats judgment-based scoring
Across several studies, subjective judgment struggles to identify future winners.


Judges favour their own group
A study of court rulings in Kenya found that defendants were more likely to win if they shared the judge’s ethnicity or gender.
Chen, Daniel L., et al., “Do Judges Favour Their Own Ethnicity and Gender?” (2022).


Judges do not beat a simple survey
In a business plan competition, a short applicant survey predicted future firm growth slightly better than expert judge panels did on their own.
Fafchamps, Marcel, and Christopher Woodruff, “Identifying gazelles: Expert panels vs. surveys,” World Bank Economic Review 31(3) (2017).


Judges, and algorithms, both struggle
Comparing judges’ scores, researcher prediction models, and machine learning in a Nigerian business competition, none of the three approaches predicted which firms actually survived, grew, or turned a profit three years later.
McKenzie, David, and Dario Sansone, “Predicting entrepreneurial success is hard,” Journal of Development Economics 141 (2019).



Subjective judgment, even from experts, struggles to reliably pick future winners. This is part of why rules-based methods – lotteries or scored cutoffs – are often the fairer and more defensible way to allocate a programme, rather than discretionary picks.

Multiple treatment arms: testing programme versions
Randomly assign firms (or CEOs, employees) to different versions of the programme, and compare them against each other and against the comparison group. This also works without a comparison group at all, if you only want to compare versions.
Best when: you’re uncertain which component or design actually drives results, and want to know which version works best, not just whether the programme works.
Advantage: helps investigate the channels of impact. Trade-off: needs a larger sample size, since it’s split across more groups.

section: Randomised phase-in: everyone gets it, just not at once
text:
Randomised phase-in: everyone gets it, just not at once
Everybody eventually receives the programme, just at different, randomly assigned times. Whoever is scheduled last serves as the comparison group in the meantime. Leave enough time between waves for impacts to develop.
Best when: budget, time, or capacity constraints mean you can’t roll the programme out to everyone at once.
Advantages: everyone eventually receives the programme, which makes the decision transparent and easier to justify; it also lets you study how impact changes with different treatment durations. Trade-off: you can’t observe long-term impacts, since the comparison group eventually receives the programme too.

section: Randomised intensities: varying how much firms get
text:
Randomised intensities: varying how much firms get
Randomly vary how much of the programme each firm gets: for example, some firms get it for 100% of eligible employees, others for only part, e.g. 50%, and others none at all (the comparison group).
Best when: spillovers are likely – for example, information spreading between treated and untreated employees within the same firm.
Advantage: lets you analyse possible spillovers, not just the direct effect. Trade-off: needs a bigger sample size to detect effects at each intensity level.

title: How
section: Facing low take-up? Randomise the encouragement
text:
Facing low take-up? Randomise the encouragement
The problem: low take-up. The firms who need a programme most can be the least likely to take it up – badly managed firms often don’t know they’re badly managed. Low take-up also makes it hard to tell whether a programme is working.
Solution: encouragement design. When you can’t deny the programme to anyone – for example, an open voucher scheme – randomise who gets extra outreach or information encouraging them to take it up, then compare the encouraged group with the not-encouraged group.
Advantage: works even when everyone must have access to the programme. Trade-off: only captures part of the impact, and can be biased if untargeted encouragement – TV or radio, for example – reaches the comparison group too.

Compliance is rarely perfect: some encouraged firms never take up the programme, and some not-encouraged firms take it up anyway. Compare the whole encouraged group with the whole not-encouraged group regardless.

title: How
section: Still not convinced? More arguments for randomising
text:
Still not convinced? More arguments for randomising


Free and fair competition
The researcher determines allocation, not personal connections or favouritism, so there’s no selection bias – no systematic difference between groups on average. It can be designed to answer precisely the question you need answered, especially when the effect of a policy is uncertain.


Equality and non-discrimination
Often the outcome of a policy isn’t clear, and it could even be negative. Testing first, rather than rolling it out to everyone, protects people from that uncertainty. You can also make sure everyone still receives the core programme, and only randomise an add-on whose effect isn’t yet known.


Publicity and transparency
A randomised design needs fewer additional assumptions than other evaluation methods. Because the analysis is less complex, it’s easier to explain and defend the findings to the people affected by them.

section: You need evidence on what is actually worth funding
text:
You need evidence on what is actually worth funding
The EU is one of the world’s largest investors in innovation. Research and innovation got roughly a tenth of its €361 billion Cohesion Policy budget for 2021–2027. Yet regional gaps in innovation outcomes are holding back the EU’s competitiveness. To keep pace with global competitors, every euro invested needs to deliver more.
Cohesion policy programmes often do not learn as they go. But policies need to adapt as circumstances change. That means identifying challenges, testing solutions, and refining approaches.

This is what we call science-based adaptive delivery: testing, learning, and adjusting as you go.

title: Join a growing community of practice for experimental evaluation in Europe
section: Randomised controlled trials show what works and why
text:
Randomised controlled trials show what works and why
By comparing what happens with support to what would have happened without it, a randomised controlled trial shows whether a cohesion policy programme is really the reason things improved. A programme built this way can adjust as conditions change, instead of running on assumptions made once and never tested.
Piloting a new idea at small scale is the best way to test it. For this, the evaluation needs to be designed ex-ante, before the call for proposals launches.

section: But what is impact evaluation exactly?
text:
But what is impact evaluation exactly?

It allows us to answer the questions: what impact did this intervention have on regional development, and how did different approaches change the outcome? For whom did it work best, and under which conditions?

To answer that, an impact evaluation isolates a program’s actual effect from everything else going on (economic trends, other policies, or the kinds of firms likely to apply in the first place), rather than just describing what happened. It compares what actually happened after introducing a program to what would have happened without it, the counterfactual.


Not the same as M&E
M&E tracks whether a program is implemented as planned. Impact evaluation tests whether it caused a real difference, compared to what would have happened without it.


Built in from day one
The comparison group, sample size, and data collection all depend on decisions made before a program launches, not added on afterward.


Each one builds on the last
Each evaluation answers some questions and raises new ones, helping you understand your regional market and design more impactful programs next time.

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
text: The groundwork a Managing Authority needs before fieldwork can start.

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
text:
Overview
Before any data is collected and before any evaluation contract is signed, a Managing Authority needs to be clear about three things: what the program is trying to achieve, how progress toward that goal will be measured, and what data will be needed to do so. This page walks through those three steps in sequence.

Step 1: Define a Theory of Change for your evaluation
Step 2: Build relevant indicators
Step 3: Choose your data strategy

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
section: Step 1: Define a Theory of Change
text:
Step 1: Define a Theory of Change

What is a Theory of Change — and how does it relate to your intervention logic?
Managing Authorities preparing ERDF or ESF+ programmes are already required to articulate an intervention logic — a structured account of how a policy instrument is expected to produce its intended results. A Theory of Change (ToC) builds on this familiar concept and makes it more explicit and evaluation-ready.
Where an intervention logic maps the pathway from inputs to outputs to results, a ToC adds two important elements: it specifies the assumptions that must hold at each step for the logic to work, and it makes clear which links in the chain are strong and which are uncertain. This is precisely the information an impact evaluation is designed to test.
If your program already has a well-developed intervention logic in its program document or partnership agreement, you have a strong starting point. The task of building a ToC is largely one of making that logic more precise — defining each step clearly enough that it can be measured.


Components of a Theory of Change
A ToC follows a causal chain from resources invested to long-term change achieved, with assumptions sitting at every junction:
Inputs are the resources, efforts, and actions invested in a policy — financial resources, personnel, equipment, and training program. For ERDF programs, inputs typically include ERDF co-financing, national co-financing, and the administrative capacity of the Managing Authority and intermediate bodies.
Activities are the concrete actions undertaken to deliver the program — running grant calls, disbursing subsidies, delivering advisory services, or providing vouchers for technology adoption. These are what the program actually does.
Outputs are the direct, countable results of those activities — the number of firms supported, grants awarded, training hours delivered, or innovation projects launched. Outputs are what the program produces. For ERDF programs, these correspond closely to the common output indicators (COIs) that Managing Authorities are already required to report to the European Commission.
Short-term outcomes are the immediate changes that occur as a direct result of the outputs — for example, a supported firm adopting a new technology, or a researcher filing a patent application. These changes typically occur within one to two years of support and are often related to shifts in knowledge, behaviour, or capacity among beneficiaries.
Medium-term outcomes are the broader changes that emerge as short-term outcomes accumulate — for example, increases in firm-level productivity, growth in exports, or improvements in the regional innovation ecosystem. These correspond closely to the common result indicators (CRIs) that ERDF and ESF+ programmes report on, though impact evaluations typically aim to go further by establishing a credible causal link between the program and the result.
Goals are the long-term aspirations of the policy — for a competitiveness programme, this might mean a more innovative regional economy, higher wages, or greater resilience to economic shocks. Goals typically require years to materialise and reflect the broader objectives of the Smart Specialisation Strategy or the national reform agenda.
Assumptions are the conditions that must hold for each link in the causal chain to lead to the next. For example, a grant scheme assumes that firms face genuine financial constraints that prevent them from investing in innovation without support. If that assumption does not hold — if firms would have innovated anyway — the program may produce outputs without producing real outcomes. Making assumptions explicit tells you where the logic is most likely to break and what an impact evaluation needs to test.


Why Invest Time in Developing a Theory of Change?
Developing a ToC is well worth the effort for two important reasons. First, it sharpens the design of your evaluation. By mapping out the causal logic of an intervention, a ToC generates clear research questions and helps teams identify which outcomes to measure and what data to collect. It can be built collaboratively — by starting from the desired final outcomes and working backwards through the chain of events needed to get there — and this process is particularly useful in a program partnership context, where multiple stakeholders may have different views on how the policy is supposed to work. It also prompts a credibility check: is there actually evidence, from comparable programs in other regions or member states, to support each step in the logic?
Second, a ToC produces richer and more transferable policy lessons. Measuring the right intermediate outcomes reveals not just whether an intervention worked, but how and why it worked. Opening this “black box” transforms evaluation results from a simple pass/fail verdict into actionable insight that can inform the next programming period. The knowledge gained also travels better — findings grounded in a clear causal logic are more readily applied by other Managing Authorities facing similar challenges in different regional contexts.


Defining Evaluation Questions
Defining clear evaluation questions is the starting point of any rigorous impact evaluation, and they should follow directly from the ToC. A well-formulated evaluation question specifies what the intervention is, who it targets, what outcome is expected to change, and over what time horizon.
Evaluation questions should be realistic: they must be answerable with the data and methods available, and scoped to what the evaluation can credibly attribute to the program rather than to external factors such as macroeconomic trends or parallel national schemes. Setting these questions before the program launches — ideally before the first call for applications — is essential, because many of the data collection decisions that follow depend on them.

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
text:
Step 2: Build Relevant Indicators

From Theory of Change to Indicators
Once the ToC is in place, it becomes the blueprint for selecting indicators. Every element of the ToC — inputs, activities, outputs, short- and medium-term outcomes, goals, and assumptions — needs at least one measurable indicator to track whether things are moving as expected.
For Managing Authorities, some of this work is already done. ERDF and ESF+ programmes operate within a mandatory performance framework that includes common output and result indicators set by the European Commission. These provide a useful starting point, but they are generally not sufficient for an impact evaluation. Common indicators are designed for monitoring — they tell you what was delivered — but an evaluation also needs to measure what changed as a result, and to do so in a way that allows for comparison with a counterfactual (i.e., what would have happened without the program).
Indicators for evaluation purposes therefore need to go beyond the mandatory monitoring set and capture the intermediate and final outcomes described in the ToC.


Well-Defined Indicators
Good indicators share five characteristics, often summarised as SMART:







Criterion
Description




Specific
The indicator measures exactly the construct it is supposed to measure — not a proxy that is merely convenient


Measurable
The information can be reliably obtained, ideally in a numerical form that allows for comparison over time and across groups


Attributable
The indicator is sensitive to the program’s efforts and not so heavily influenced by external factors that changes cannot be attributed to the intervention


Realistic
The data can be obtained within the available time and budget, at a frequency that matches the evaluation timeline


Targeted
The indicator reflects outcomes for the specific population the program is designed to serve




Running example. TO BE ADDED BY MIKE: Indicators from the North-East



From Indicators to Data
Indicators rarely need to be built from scratch. Managing Authorities should draw on existing, well-tested measures from comparable evaluations before designing new ones. Validated frameworks such as the Community Innovation Survey (CIS), the World Bank Enterprise Surveys, or the OECD Oslo Manual provide internationally comparable definitions and question formats that have been tested across many contexts. Using them improves the quality of your data and makes findings easier to compare with evidence from other programs and regions.
Once indicators are defined, each one requires a concrete data source. The next step answers — for every indicator — what needs to be collected, what type of data is appropriate, how it should be gathered, from whom, and when. Crucially, all of these decisions must be made before the program launches and before randomization begins. Data collected as an afterthought rarely has the properties needed for a credible evaluation.

Selecting the right indicators is easier when you can draw on a curated list of outcomes that have already been used in comparable firm-level impact evaluations. The EuroComp Lab Outcomes Bank provides a searchable reference of outcome indicators organised by topic — covering firm performance, innovation, R&D, technology adoption, digitalisation, management capacities, collaboration, intellectual property, access to finance, employment, market performance, and environmental sustainability.
For each outcome, the bank specifies: - A plain-language definition - The metric and unit of measurement - Whether primary survey data or administrative data is the most appropriate source

📋 Browse the Outcomes Bank →

The bank is organised to mirror the topics covered in the Survey Question Bank on the companion page, making it straightforward to move from selecting an outcome to identifying the survey question that measures it.

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
text:
Step 3: Choose Your Data Strategy

The Fundamental Decision
Before any fieldwork begins, the most consequential data decision is a strategic one: for each indicator in your evaluation framework, will you rely on primary data collected specifically for the evaluation, secondary data that already exists in administrative records, or a combination of both?
This is not primarily a technical question — it is a practical and resource question that the Managing Authority and its evaluation team must answer together, ideally before the program is designed.
Primary data is information collected directly from target respondents — firms, individuals, or organisations — through surveys or interviews conducted specifically for the evaluation. It gives you control over exactly what is measured, but it takes time and money to collect, and it places a burden on beneficiaries.
Secondary data draws on records that already exist — national business registries, tax authority data, customs records, patent office databases, or the program’s own management information system. Secondary data is generally cheaper and covers larger samples, but it may not include the specific outcome variables needed for an evaluation and often comes with reporting lags or access restrictions.
In practice, the most robust evaluations combine both: secondary administrative data provides the baseline and ensures broad coverage, while primary survey data captures the outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain. Deciding early which data sources will fill which role in the evaluation is essential — and it shapes every subsequent design choice.

Assessing What You Already Have
Before commissioning a new survey, Managing Authorities should take stock of the administrative data they already hold or can access. Program management systems typically record beneficiary characteristics, grant amounts, payment dates, and reported output indicators. National statistical offices, tax authorities, business registries, and customs agencies hold firm-level data on turnover, employment, exports, and tax payments — often going back many years, which is particularly valuable for establishing pre-intervention baselines.
The key question is whether these sources contain — or can be linked to contain — the specific outcome variables in the evaluation framework. If a firm’s VAT number or national registration number is collected at application stage, it may be possible to link program records to tax or registry data using that identifier, enabling outcome measurement without any additional data collection burden on beneficiaries.


Planning Data Collection
Once the data strategy is set, detailed planning for each data collection activity should address the following:
What to collect should be driven strictly by the indicators in the ToC. Data collected for its own sake — without a clear link to an evaluation question — adds cost and respondent burden without adding analytical value.
Who to collect from should match the unit of analysis. For firm-level program, this typically means the firm itself, represented by a senior decision-maker who can speak reliably to strategic and financial outcomes. Where the program targets a specific group within the firm — such as R&D staff or recently hired employees — those individuals may be the more appropriate respondents for certain questions.
When to collect must align with the evaluation timeline. Baseline data must be collected before the intervention begins. Endline data should be timed to when effects can realistically be expected to have materialised — too early, and real impacts may not yet be visible. Intermediate rounds may be needed to track progress along the Theory of Change.

text:
EuroCOMP Lab evaluations
Full case studies for each project, deeper than the wanted posters on How.

Running example. Romania runs through every page of the site. This is where the full story sits, with the baseline report attached.


Financial support to digitalize: Romania’s program provides non-refundable grants to SMEs for digitalization, aiming to boost productivity in the North-East region, with a focus on key digital performance indicators. Digitalization has the potential to transform industries, particularly SMEs, which in Romania lag behind the EU average in digital performance. Key barriers to digital transformation include lack of financing, awareness, and capacity to capitalize on digital investments. In North-East Romania, digitalization grants are awarded to eligible SMEs under the de minimis aid scheme, with a total allocation ofA C31,000,000 in the first call (A C26,350,000 ERDF andA C4,650,000 from the state budget). Firms can receive grants ranging fromA C15,000 toA C100,000, covering 90% of eligible project costs. The World Bank studies the impact of digitalization on SME performance. The hypothesis is that financial support will boost productivity by enabling the acquisition of knowledge, services, and soft/hardware. As part of the study, the World Bank conducted a pre-assessment using DESI indicators, as defined by the Regional Development Agency (RDA): The most common technology was “20+ percent of employees using connected mobile devices” (681 businesses, 66% of the sample), followed by “Internet connection of at least 30 Megabits per second” (620 businesses, 60%) and “50+ percent of employees with Internet access” (604 businesses, 58%).


Financial support to innovate: Spain’s matching grant program awards up toA C250k per firm to boost R&D investment in small and medium companies, primarily in agriculture and ecological transition.  To address market failures that keep regional R&D investment at suboptimal levels, the La Junta de Extremadura, the Regional Government of Extremadura (JUNTA) and Foundation for the Development of Science and Technology and the Extremadura Science and Technology Park Foundation (FUNDECYT-PCTEx) have developed a matching grant program funded by the EU, offering large R&D grants to small and medium firms in Extremadura. Each cycle plans to awardA C3.5 million in grants (up to C250k per company), financing 35% to 80% of proposed R&D investments. Applicants are primarily small and medium companies, mainly in the agricultural or ecological transition sectors, with most grants supporting industrial research and experimental development. The World Bank is collaborating with JUNTA to offer technical support aimed at generating valuable insights from this investment. In this process, the evaluation team, working with regional authorities, has revised operational manuals to enhance the institutional framework by incorporating international best practices in the design, implementation, and evaluation of this public instrument.


Add-Ons to make financial support more impactful: In Czechia, the World Bank evaluates whether enhancing entrepreneurial skills improves the effectiveness of a voucher scheme supporting business development, innovation, and digital transformation in regions affected by the coal industry’s decline.  Several Czech regions are focused on economic diversification, prioritizing private sector growth, but entrepreneurial activity remains low. A new program, approved by the European Commission in September 2022, targets regions affected by the decline of the coal mining industry. It emphasizes business R&D, post-mining area regeneration, skills development, clean energy, and the circular economy, with a total allocation ofA C1.641 billion. A key component of the Just Transition Programme (JTP) is the voucher scheme for entrepreneurs in Czech coal regions, offering different types of financial support. These vouchers are available in the Moravian-Silesian, Ustí, and Karlovy Vary regions, with a focus on diversifying local economies reliant on carbon intensive industries. The impact evaluation includes complementary activities to strengthen the JTP outcomes. One such initiative is the ‘Smart Start’ project, launched with World Bank’s support since 2022. In the Ustí and Karlovy Vary regions, this program focuses on innovation vouchers, incorporating a ‘networking’ approach, where firms receive expert advisory support and are encouraged to share knowledge and network to enhance innovation. In the Moravian-Silesian region, the program emphasizes mindset training for innovation, offering ‘smart training’ that promotes a scientific approach to decision-making under uncertainty. This training, aimed at firms selected for entrepreneurial vouchers (and others), teaches participants to make informed decisions in uncertain environments, covering topics such as understanding innovation, risk vs. uncertainty, hypothesis testing, and A/B testing, culminating in participant presentations.


AMatchmaking support to connect: The Scinergy pilot in Croatia connects businesses and scientists to foster collaborations, support innovation, and drive R&D through matchmaking events and ongoing guidance.  A World Bank survey revealed that 47% of companies lacked information about relevant scientists, highlighting the need for improved collaboration to drive innovation and technology transfer. To strengthen science-business collaboration, Croatia is piloting a business-science matchmaking support program. For this purpose, the World Bank, in partnership with the Innovation Center Nikola Tesla and the Ministry of Science, Education, and Youth, designed the “Scinergy” pilot to facilitate science-business collaboration. Scinergy aims to help connect businesses and scientists based on their needs and expertise, supporting product development, joint funding applications, and public-private partnerships. Participating firms are offered targeted connections with scientists across fields like AI, energy, and biotechnology, and are offered legal and communication support. Matched researchers and businesses first participated in a two-day matchmaking event in February 2024. The first day involved “speed-dating” sessions between firms and scientists, while the second day featured workshops for pairs interested in collaboration. These sessions encouraged ideation, with exercises like explaining potential solutions in simple terms and visualizing them through drawings. In March and April 2024, these pairs explored concrete R&D ideas, leading to detailed discussions and joint project planning. Pilot monitoring revealed that newly established interactions between firms and scientists continued in this period, with discussions on collaboration details, intellectual property, legal frameworks, and project financing. Firms attended specialized lectures on these topics, which deepened their understanding and aimed to facilitate cooperation. Qualitative insights and feedback surveys from participants indicated that the main collaboration goals were joint R&D projects, technological consultations, and prototype development. Companies reported challenges such as financial constraints, legal issues, and aligning goals.

text: This page covers why evaluation is worth doing, when it has to be decided, and how to choose between the available designs.

title: Why and When
text:
What is impact evaluation for?


  
  Impact evaluation

Learning feeds programme design. Accountability covers both what the money was spent on and what it achieved.

title: Why and When
section: Testing and learning only works if you know what to look for
text:
Testing and learning only works if you know what to look for
When evaluating projects, we often only assess outputs, because they are the easiest thing to count. Impact evaluation is what lets you move from measuring outputs to proving outcomes.


Outputs
What a programme delivers: grants disbursed, firms enrolled, trainings run.


Outcomes
What changes because of it: growth, jobs, innovation, resilience.


Before implementation, map out how a programme’s activities are expected to change the problem you are addressing. That shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next. That causal logic, the how and why behind each step, explains a program’s reason for existing. It also tells you what to measure to test whether the expected change is actually happening.


Inputs


Activities


Outputs


Outcomes


This chain is the foundation of a Theory of Change, and having thought it through helps in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in Theory of Change, Indicators and Data.

title: Why and When
section: Learning through impact evaluation is a continuous process
text:
Learning through impact evaluation is a continuous process
Every evaluation raises new questions along with the ones it answers, each round building on the last. That is how we expand our knowledge of what works, for whom, and under what conditions, and use it to design better programmes. Exchange within a community of practice matters, so we can learn from each other, not just from our own results.


  
    
      
    
  
  
  
  
  

  
  Design

  
  Test

  
  Review evidence,
  create learnings

  
  Adjust and invest




Review Review a programme’s theory of change, identify risks and learning opportunities. Review lessons from other settings and countries, adapt them, test them in a new context. Identify baseline needs of potential beneficiaries in your region.


Test Test different programme designs and delivery modes to identify what works best. Assess for whom the programme works best. Address take-up challenges, both over and undersubscription. Learn about mechanisms, unintended effects, and crowding out.


Invest Get a quantitative and credible impact estimate that can guide future investments. Conduct cost-benefit analyses to avoid wasting money and to inform programme decisions. Scale up based on evidence.



The running example: SMART Romania
Throughout this site, we come back to one programme developed as part of the EuroCOMP Lab to show these ideas in practice: SMART Romania, a digitalisation grant scheme for micro, small and medium enterprises in North-East Romania, run by the Regional Development Agency with World Bank support.

  WhereNorth-East Romania; run by the regional development agency with World Bank support
  Who is randomizedFirms: 1,038 eligible MSMEs, pre-screened via an online application survey
  The designLottery into a treatment group (grants) and a comparison group: 519 vs. 519, drawn before a notary
  Outcomes trackedDigital adoption (DESI), revenues, profits, employment, productivity

Is it relevant for you

title: Why and When
section: Think impact evaluation is not relevant for you?
text:
Think impact evaluation is not relevant for you?
Whether you have sufficient evidence that your programme works, or you are still working out who it reaches and how to design it, there is a case for evaluation. The starting question is whether the programme is working as well as it could be.



You want to learn who to target and how to design it


Too many applicants? Consider introducing randomisation in the middle ranks.
Too few applicants? Consider simplifying access and using an encouragement design.




You know it is effective, but is it efficient?


Test how you deliver it. Compare different ways of delivering the programme to the same beneficiaries, testing changes that improve efficiency and satisfaction.




An impact evaluation is not useful only if you already have enough evidence on returns for your target group and region, and there is no interest in learning about different ways of implementing the programme for the same beneficiaries.


M&E versus impact evaluation

title: Why and When
section: Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation
text:
Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation



Monitoring


Collect data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to

Improve day-to-day management and decisions
Make descriptive before and after comparisons



Describes what is happening, but not whether it is because of the intervention.




Impact evaluation


Collect data on participants and control groups to

Assess the difference between participating and not
Establish causality
Support cost-benefit analysis



Determines impact in a way that can only be attributed to the programme, by establishing what would have happened without it.




Allocating public resources

title: Why and When
section: What does good allocation of public resources look like?
text:
What does good allocation of public resources look like?
Not always what you would expect at first glance. Impact evaluation can help improve allocation.



Strategy A: fund the top performers


Firms that succeed: 80 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 65
Caused by the grant: 15


Looks stronger: 80 successes.




Strategy B: fund the marginal firm


Firms that succeed: 55 of 100
Would have succeeded anyway: 20
Caused by the grant: 35


Actually causes more impact: 35 caused.

  Strategy A

  
  55

  Strategy B

  
  Observed successes
  
  Caused by the grant

Raw success counts can be misleading. Programmes should be judged on impact, not on the raw success of hand-picked winners.



Deadweight: low additionality
Additionality’ is the share of activity that wouldn’t have happened without the programme. Top performers would likely have invested anyway, so public funds mostly substitute for money they’d have spent regardless — generating little that’s truly additional per euro.


Selection bias in measurement
Comparing funded, stronger firms with unfunded, weaker ones credits the programme with firms’ pre-existing quality, not with what the grant did.


Where the grant buys most
Support actually changes behaviour for the marginal, constrained firm: the good project that could not otherwise get funded.



The counterfactual

title: Why and When
section: What exactly is the impact of a programme?
text:
What exactly is the impact of a programme?
Definition. Impact is what happens after a programme is introduced, minus what would have happened in its absence, the counterfactual.
The dilemma. The counterfactual is a “what if” and is unknown to us.
The solution. Find a way to construct the counterfactual so impact can be measured. This can be done in different ways. The methods below show why randomised controlled trials are considered the gold standard.

  Counterfactual

Impact is the causal effect of the programme: the gap between what happened and what would have happened.


The impact in the SMART Romania programme
For SMART Romania, the impact is the gap between treatment and comparison firms on four tracked outcomes: digital adoption, revenue, employment, and productivity.

title: Why and When
text:
Finding the counterfactual
Strategy. Find a group of firms that on average look like treated firms would have looked in the absence of the programme. This group is the comparison group.



Randomised controlled trials


Create the comparison group up front, by randomly assigning who receives the programme. Randomisation is what guarantees the two groups look the same on average.




Ex-post and quasi-experimental designs


Look for a suitable comparison group after the programme has already been rolled out, using natural variation in who received it and who did not.




Selection bias is the risk that the comparison group does not actually look like the treatment group on average. If that assumption is wrong, the impact estimate is biased.


SMART Romania: what is the counterfactual?
In SMART Romania, the counterfactual is represented by the firms that completed the online survey and were deemed eligible but that did not receive the grant.
Before any grants were awarded, the selected and non-selected groups looked statistically the same: identical average DESI score (4.3 of 12), similar firm size, no significant difference overall. That balance is what makes the non-selected group a credible stand-in for what the selected firms would have done without the programme.


Randomised controlled trials

title: Why and When
section: What is a randomised controlled trial?
text:
What is a randomised controlled trial?
Intuition. Randomly assign the programme so one group receives it (the treatment group) and one does not (the control or comparison group). Because the two groups start out the same, the control group’s outcome shows what would have happened to the treatment group without the programme.

Advantage. RCTs are considered the gold standard of quantitative impact evaluation because:

No assumptions about outcome levels or trends between groups are necessary, if randomised within groups
They deliver strong evidence
They are easy to interpret

Because the lottery created two comparable groups, the difference between them over time is the impact ofbeing of the program.

title: Why and When
section: Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes
text:
Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes
Randomly selecting beneficiaries among eligible applicants is fair. When more eligible firms apply than there is budget to fund, a lottery is a transparent way to decide who gets in. It treats every eligible applicant the same rather than relying on favouritism or timing.

When you cannot randomize

title: Why and When
text:
What if you cannot randomise?
An RCT only works if randomization is built in from day one, integrated at design stage before the programme launches, not added afterward. The comparison group, sample size, and data to collect all depend on those early decisions. When that is not possible, quasi-experimental methods are the alternative.

Quasi-experimental methods always rely on assumptions, some stronger than others. If those assumptions do not hold, the impact estimate is biased. Many of these assumptions are not testable. The credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of the assumptions made.


Pre-post (before and after)


Method

Compare programme participants before and after the programme.

Identifying assumption

In the absence of the programme, participants would have had the same measured outcomes as before. That means no other factors or events, for example economic shocks, affect the outcome besides the programme. This is a strong assumption that rarely holds in practice.



For example, sales might rise after a grant simply because the whole regional economy is recovering at the same time, not because of the programme.

There are no differences between participants and matched non-participants in unobserved characteristics that affect the outcome.



For example, two firms matched on size and sector might still differ in the owner’s ambition or management quality, both of which would likely affect outcomes.

This does not measure impact for all participants, only for those at the cut-off, which is why the result is called a local average treatment effect. Risks

title: Why and When
section: What can go wrong with a well-designed RCT?
text:
What can go wrong with a well-designed RCT?


01

Non-compliance and take-up
Not every firm assigned to a programme ends up participating. Comparing everyone as originally assigned (the intention-to-treat effect) stays unbiased, since assignment was random, but it understates the effect on those who actually participated.



02

Attrition
Participants may drop out before outcomes can be measured, or stop responding to follow-up data collection. The risk is that dropout is not random: if struggling firms are the ones most likely to disappear, the firms you do measure make the programme look better than it is.



03

Spillovers and contamination
The comparison group is not always as isolated as it looks. Know-how from a business training programme can spread by word of mouth to non-participating competitors or suppliers, so the comparison group partly benefits too, understating the true effect.




SMART Romania: the programme did not achieve full take-up
Of the 519 firms selected by lottery, only 393 (75.7%) went on to submit a full funding proposal, and 333 (64.2%) were eventually contracted.
Because of limited take-up, it is safer to report the intention-to-treat effect, comparing everyone as originally assigned, even though it understates the effect on the firms that actually took up the grant.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text: How to design and implement a primary data collection exercise once your evaluation framework is in place.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Overview
This page picks up where the [Theory of Change and Measurement] page leaves off. Once a Managing Authority has defined its Theory of Change (ToC), selected its outcome indicators, and decided that primary data collection is needed, the practical question becomes: how do you actually go out and collect it?
The answer, in most evaluation contexts, is a survey. This page explains what surveys are, why they are well-suited to the evaluation needs, and — most importantly — how to design and implement one well. It covers the choice of collection method, the design of the questionnaire, respondent selection, timing, and the legal obligations that apply under EU data protection law.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Why Surveys?
Surveys are the most widely used tool for collecting primary data in impact evaluations of public support programs. They make it possible to gather structured, comparable information directly from the firms, individuals, or organisations that a program is designed to benefit — capturing precisely the outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain.
A particular strength of surveys is their scalability. Rather than collecting information from every single beneficiary or firm in a target population, a well-designed survey can be conducted on a carefully selected subset — known as a sample — and, provided that sample is representative, the findings can be generalised with confidence to the full population. For Managing Authorities overseeing programs with hundreds or thousands of beneficiaries, this makes surveys a practical and cost-effective route to credible evidence.
For programs evaluating competitiveness and innovation outcomes — such as changes in firm-level R&D investment, technology adoption, or export performance — surveys are often the only way to capture the intermediate outcomes that sit between a grant payment (recorded in program management systems) and a long-term productivity gain (visible, eventually, in national statistics). They are also essential for understanding why an intervention worked or did not, by measuring the mechanisms — changes in knowledge, capacity, or behaviour — that link the program’s activities to its results.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Paper vs. Electronic Surveys
Surveys can be conducted on paper or in electronic form. While paper-based surveys remain in use in some contexts, electronic surveys are the clear standard for program evaluations today and should be the default choice for Managing Authorities.
Digital surveys offer substantial practical advantages. They allow for built-in data validation — mandatory fields, range checks, and logical skip patterns — which means that errors and inconsistencies are caught at the point of entry rather than discovered during analysis. They eliminate the transcription step entirely: responses flow directly into a dataset, ready for processing. They are faster to deploy, easier to monitor in real time, and considerably simpler to adapt if pilot testing reveals problems with specific questions.
For Managing Authorities working within tight program timelines and reporting deadlines, the efficiency gains from digital collection are significant.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Choosing a Collection Method
There is no single best method for electronic data collection. The right choice depends on who the respondents are, what the questions require, and what budget is available. Three methods are in common use:
Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) involves trained interviewers conducting structured surveys over the phone, guided by a digital questionnaire on their screen. CATI can reach a broad range of respondents relatively quickly and is well-suited to situations where response rates need to be actively managed — interviewers can follow up with non-respondents and clarify questions in real time. It is also a practical option when beneficiary contact details (phone numbers) are already held in program management systems. The main limitations are cost, the need to recruit and train interviewers, and the constraint that surveys must be kept short enough to hold a respondent’s attention on the phone.
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) takes the form of face-to-face interviews conducted with the support of a tablet or laptop loaded with survey software. The key advantage is the quality of responses: the personal interaction between interviewer and respondent tends to produce more nuanced and accurate answers, particularly on sensitive topics such as firm finances, employment decisions, or the perceived impact of public support. CAPI is also effective when the questionnaire is long or complex. The trade-offs are cost — travel and interviewer time make CAPI the most expensive method — and the risk that the interviewer’s presence influences how respondents answer. This method is best reserved for situations where data quality is the overriding priority and the sample is relatively small and geographically concentrated.
Web surveys are questionnaires sent to respondents via email or embedded in an online platform, inviting them to complete the survey at a time and pace that suits them. They are the least expensive method and can be deployed quickly to large samples. For programs targeting SMEs, research organisations, or technology firms — populations that are generally comfortable with online tools — web surveys are often the most practical choice. The main risk is response bias: firms or individuals without reliable internet access, or those with less time available, may be less likely to respond, potentially skewing results. Response rates for unsolicited web surveys are also often low, so active follow-up is typically needed.
In practice, methods can be combined. A common approach is to begin with a web survey, follow up with CATI for non-respondents, and use CAPI selectively for specific subgroups where richer qualitative detail is needed.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Designing the Survey

Start with What Already Exists
Before writing a single question, Managing Authorities and their evaluation teams should review existing, validated survey instruments. Using questions that have already been tested and used in comparable evaluations saves time, improves data quality, and — critically — makes findings comparable with evidence from other programs and regions. Relevant reference sources include:

The Community Innovation Survey (CIS), which provides the standard EU framework for measuring innovation activity in firms and is used across all member states
The Firms Adoption of Technology Survey (FAT), a World Bank instrument covering how firms adopt, use, and benefit from technologies across sectors
The World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES), which cover a wide range of firm-level outcomes including investment, productivity, and the business environment
The World Management Survey (WMS), which measures the quality of management practices across firms and countries and has been shown to be a strong predictor of firm productivity and innovation
The Flash Eurobarometer on SME Digitalisation, which tracks digital technology adoption, online sales, and digital skills across EU member states
The ECB Survey on Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE), which monitors financing conditions and constraints for SMEs across the euro area
The OECD Oslo Manual, which defines innovation concepts and measurement approaches in a way that is consistent across countries
Survey instruments used in published evaluations of comparable ERDF or ESF+ programs in other regions or member states



To make this process as practical as possible, the EuroComp Lab has compiled a Survey Question Bank — a ready-to-use library of validated questions drawn from the Community Innovation Survey (CIS), the World Bank Firms Adoption of Technology (FAT) Survey, the World Bank Enterprise Surveys, the World Management Survey (WMS), and the Flash Eurobarometer on SME Digitalisation, among others.

Where program-specific questions need to be developed — for example, to capture the specific features of a regional grant scheme — they should be designed to complement rather than replace validated instruments.


Questionnaire Design
A good questionnaire is clear, concise, and purposeful. Every question should have a direct link to an indicator in the ToC. Questions included for general interest, or because the data might be useful someday, add burden for respondents without adding analytical value and should be removed.
Questions should address only one idea at a time. So-called double-barrelled questions — which ask about two things simultaneously, such as “Did the grant improve your firm’s R&D capacity and export performance?” — make it impossible for respondents to give an accurate answer and should always be avoided. Wording should be neutral: leading questions that steer respondents towards a particular answer undermine the reliability of the data and should be eliminated during the review process.
Response scales — such as Likert scales or numerical ratings — should be consistent across the questionnaire and clearly labelled. Questions should flow in a logical sequence, moving from general topics to more specific ones. Sensitive questions — such as those about turnover, profitability, or employment figures — are best placed towards the end, once some rapport has been established with the respondent.
Questions that ask about quantities, values, or periods of time should always specify the unit and reference period explicitly. Ambiguity about whether turnover should be reported in thousands or millions of euros, whether employment refers to full-time equivalents or headcount, or whether “last year” means the calendar year or the most recent financial year leads to inconsistent responses that are difficult to clean and compare. Each such question should state the currency (e.g., €), the unit of magnitude (e.g., full-time equivalents, thousands of euros), and the exact time reference (e.g., “in the last financial year, ending [month]”) directly in the question text or as a visible instruction above the response field.
Where surveys are to be conducted in multiple languages — a common situation for programs operating across linguistically diverse regions, or for evaluations coordinated across member states — the questionnaire should be professionally translated and then back-translated into the original language to verify that meaning has been preserved accurately.


Piloting the Questionnaire
No questionnaire should go into the field without first being tested. A pilot survey — conducted with a small group of respondents representative of the target population — reveals problems that are not visible on paper: ambiguous wording, questions that take too long to answer, response options that do not cover the full range of experiences, and technical glitches in digital forms. The questionnaire should be revised based on pilot findings before full deployment begins. Skipping the pilot to save time almost always costs more in the long run, through lower data quality and the need for analytical workarounds.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Who to Survey and When

Choosing the Right Respondent
The reliability of survey data depends heavily on asking the right person. The ideal respondent is someone who is knowledgeable about the outcome of interest, has little incentive to misreport, and can be reached without excessive difficulty.
For surveys targeting businesses — the most common scenario in competitiveness and innovation programs — this typically means a senior decision-maker: a CEO, CFO, or equivalent executive who has oversight of the firm’s strategic and financial decisions. Senior managers are best placed to speak to questions about investment, employment, and innovation strategy. They are also more likely to be aware of how and whether the program has influenced the firm’s trajectory.
That said, the right respondent depends on what is being measured. If the evaluation is focused on the experience of R&D personnel, or on the take-up of training by specific staff groups, those individuals may be better placed to answer certain questions than a general manager. Where possible, the respondent should be the same person at baseline and endline, to ensure that differences in answers reflect real changes rather than differences between respondents.


Timing
The timing of a survey significantly affects the quality of data collected. At the operational level, surveys targeting firm employees are best conducted during standard working hours. August is a poor time to survey firms in most European countries, due to summer holidays. The end of the financial year is also problematic, as finance teams are typically occupied with closing accounts and reporting obligations.
At the evaluation design level, the timing of surveys must be tied to the program timeline. A baseline survey must be completed before the intervention begins — and, where possible, before firms even know whether they will receive support — to avoid any contamination of pre-intervention data. The endline survey should be timed to when effects can realistically be expected to have materialised: too soon after the intervention ends, and genuine impacts may not yet be visible. Depending on the intervention, one or more intermediate surveys may also be needed to track progress along the ToC and to monitor compliance and take-up.
Managing Authorities should also be mindful of survey fatigue. Beneficiaries who are contacted repeatedly for monitoring and evaluation purposes may become less willing to participate, reducing response rates and data quality over time. Coordinating across different data collection exercises — and keeping each survey as concise as the evaluation objectives allow — helps manage this risk.

title: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Data Protection and GDPR Compliance
For EU Managing Authorities, compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is not optional — it is a legal obligation that applies to any data collection exercise involving personal data or information that could be used to identify individual firms or persons.
In practice, this means that before any survey goes into the field, the following must be in place:

A clear legal basis for processing personal data (typically the legitimate interest of the Managing Authority in evaluating public spending, or the explicit consent of respondents)
An informed consent process: respondents must be clearly told how their data will be used, how long it will be retained, and who will have access to it, before they agree to participate
Anonymisation or pseudonymisation of responses wherever possible, so that published results cannot be traced back to individual respondents or firms
Appropriate data security measures, including restricted access to identifiable data
A data protection impact assessment (DPIA), where the scale or sensitivity of the data collection warrants it

Managing Authorities should involve their data protection officer early in the evaluation design process — not as a final approval step, but as part of the initial planning. Data sharing agreements with third-party survey firms or external evaluators must also address GDPR requirements explicitly.
Beyond legal compliance, handling data responsibly also builds trust with beneficiaries. Firms and individuals who feel their information is being treated with care are more likely to participate in surveys and to answer honestly — which directly improves the quality of the evidence the evaluation produces.

text:
Use at baseline and endline. TRLs are the standard scale used by the European Commission — including in Horizon Europe and ERDF-funded R&D programmes — to assess the maturity of a technology or innovation. Measuring TRL at baseline and endline captures whether the intervention has helped firms advance their technologies along the development path from concept to market.

TRL 1 — Basic principles observed: Scientific research has begun; basic properties of the technology have been observed and reported
TRL 2 — Technology concept formulated: Application of the technology has been conceived; no experimental proof yet
TRL 3 — Experimental proof of concept: Active research and development has begun; first laboratory studies completed
TRL 4 — Technology validated in laboratory: The technology has been validated in a laboratory environment
TRL 5 — Technology validated in relevant environment: The technology has been validated in an environment relevant to its intended application (e.g. industrial simulation)
TRL 6 — Technology demonstrated in relevant environment: A prototype or pilot system has been demonstrated in a relevant environment
TRL 7 — System prototype demonstration in operational environment: The prototype is close to the planned operational system and has been demonstrated in an operational environment
TRL 8 — System complete and qualified: The technology has been proven to work in its final form and under expected conditions

A note on TRL for Managing Authorities: The TRL scale was originally developed by NASA and adapted by the European Commission for use across all Horizon Europe and ERDF R&D instruments. TRL 1–3 corresponds to basic and applied research; TRL 4–6 to technology development and validation; TRL 7–9 to demonstration and market deployment. Many EU grant schemes specify a minimum entry TRL (e.g. TRL 4 or above) and a target exit TRL, making TRL advancement a natural primary outcome for R&D support evaluations. Self-reported TRL should ideally be validated against objective evidence (e.g. prototype documentation, test reports) where possible.

title: Topic: Innovation Outputs
text:
Innovation outcomes are central to evaluations of R&D grants, technology support, and competitiveness programmes. Distinguish carefully between inputs (R&D spending) and outputs (patents, new products).
###Product innovation

Definition: Introduction of a new or significantly improved good or service
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); number of new products introduced; share of turnover from new products (%)

###Process innovation

Definition: Introduction of a new or significantly improved production, delivery, or supporting process
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); type of process innovation introduced
Data source: Primary survey (CIS-based questions)


Organisational innovation

Definition: Introduction of new organisational methods in business practices, workplace organisation, or external relations
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no)
Data source: Primary survey

Definition: Whether innovations are new only to the firm, new to the market, or new to the world — a measure of innovation ambition
Metric: Categorical (firm-level / market-level / world-level novelty)
Data source: Primary survey

Definition: The proportion of sales generated by products or services introduced in the last three years — captures commercial success of innovation

Data source: Primary survey or administrative (tax records with R&D tax credit data)

title: Advanced How
text: Designing an RCT that produces reliable evidence. Behind every successful RCT are design decisions made before the programme begins. Good randomization alone is not enough.

title: Advanced How
text:
What makes an RCT credible?
How showed the process. This page shows what separates a strong RCT from a weak one.


01

Enough firms
Groups large enough to detect real impacts.



02

Comparable groups
A lottery that actually balanced the groups.



03

Reliable outcomes
Measures that capture what matters.



04

The right design
A setup matched to the policy question.




The sections below walk through each pillar, using SMART Romania as the test case.

Enough firms›Comparable groups›Outcomes›Right design

title: Advanced How
text:
Do I have enough firms?
Randomization only works if there are enough firms to detect meaningful differences.



Too few firms







Real impacts may go undetected: ordinary differences between firms drown out the programme’s effect.




Enough firms







Real impacts become measurable: averages settle and the difference stands out.




More firms do not make the lottery fairer; they make its answer visible.

title: Advanced How
text:
Why sample size matters
How many firms are enough depends on what needs to be detected.



The size of the effect


Small effect: more firms needed.
Large effect: fewer firms needed.




The variation between firms


High variation: more firms needed.
Low variation: fewer firms needed.




Think of trying to hear a quiet voice in a noisy room: more background noise requires more observations.

title: Advanced How
section: What if there are not enough firms?
text:
What if there are not enough firms?
The most common planning problem has practical fixes.

  
    Increase outreach
    More applications mean a larger pool. SMART Romania ran events in more than 20 cities.
  
  
    Expand eligibility
    Loosen the bar so more firms qualify.
  
  
    Combine regions
    Pool similar programmes or areas into one study.
  
  
    Run a phase-in
    Everyone participates; timing creates the comparison.
  
  
    Target larger effects
    Focus the programme where impacts are biggest.
  
  
    Collect better baseline data
    Good baselines reduce noise and cut the required sample.

text:
Which outcomes should be measured?
An RCT is only as good as what it measures.



Good outcomes are



Relevant: tied to the policy objective
Measurable: data can actually be collected
Objective: not dependent on opinion
Consistent: collected the same way for every firm, every round





Measured in SMART Romania



Digital adoption (DESI)
Revenue
Employment
Productivity





Fix the outcomes before the draw: choosing them afterwards invites cherry-picking.

title: Advanced How
text:
What can go wrong?
Even a well-designed RCT must survive contact with reality.

Attrition. Firms drop out of surveys, and the groups stop matching.


Spillovers. Comparison firms benefit anyway, and the measured difference shrinks.


Low take-up. Treated firms never actually use the support.


Implementation problems. The programme is delivered unevenly across firms.

Monitoring answers all four: Data Collection.

title: Advanced How
section: When are the alternative designs worth it?
text:
When are the alternative designs worth it?
How introduced four alternative designs. The advanced question is when they earn their extra sample and complexity.


Multiple treatment arms
Choose it when: knowing which version works best matters more than sample size.


Phase-in
Choose it when: everyone must eventually receive the programme.


Randomized intensities
Choose it when: spillovers between firms or employees are the question.


Encouragement
Choose it when: access cannot be denied and take-up is the problem.

title: Topic: R&D Activity
text:
R&D outcomes are relevant for evaluations of R&D grants, Horizon Europe co-financing, and tax incentives. The key evaluation question is often additionality: does public support increase R&D spending, or does it substitute for private investment?

3.1 R&D engagement

Definition: Whether the firm conducts research and experimental development activities
Metric: Binary indicator (yes/no); frequency (continuous / occasional)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (R&D tax credit records)



3.2 R&D expenditure

Definition: Total spending on in-house and contracted-out R&D activities
Metric: Total R&D expenditure in €; share of turnover spent on R&D (%)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative (R&D tax credit records, national R&D surveys)



3.3 R&D employment

Definition: Number of staff engaged in R&D activities
Metric: Full-time equivalent (FTE) R&D staff; share of total employees in R&D roles (%)
Data source: Primary survey or administrative



3.4 R&D additionality

Definition: Whether public support leads to an increase in total R&D spending (input additionality) or new products and processes (output additionality), rather than substituting for private investment
Metric: Difference in R&D expenditure or innovation output between treatment and control groups at endline, controlling for baseline
Data source: Primary survey or administrative; requires treatment/control comparison



3.5 Patent applications

Definition: Whether the firm has applied for or obtained patents as a result of its R&D activities
Metric: Number of patent applications filed; number of patents granted; binary indicator
Data source: Administrative (EPO PATSTAT, national patent office records) or primary survey
